client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away from cancer last year. I can't seem to focus at work anymore — I'll be in the middle of something and then just... zone out, thinking about her. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: Thank you so much for being here and for taking that courageous step to try something, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that ambivalence makes complete sense given how much you're carrying. Losing your mom to cancer is a profound, life-altering grief, and what you're describing at work — that drifting away into thoughts of her — sounds like your mind is still trying to process something enormous. I'd love to understand a little more about what those moments feel like for you: when you zone out and she comes to mind, what kinds of thoughts or memories tend to surface?

client: It's usually the last few months, honestly — not the good memories, but watching her go through the treatments, how tired she looked, how I kept telling myself she was going to be okay even when the signs were there that she wasn't. I'll be staring at my computer screen and suddenly I'm back in that hospital room, and I just feel this wave of... I don't even know, guilt maybe, like I should have done something differently. It's hard to explain but it's almost like my brain won't let me just get on with things.
therapist: What you're describing sounds so painful — carrying not just the loss of her, but these vivid, intrusive images of her suffering, layered with a sense that you somehow failed her, even as you were doing your best to hold onto hope in an impossibly hard situation. That guilt you're naming is something I really want to gently explore with you, because our minds can sometimes hold us responsible for things that were never truly in our control. When that feeling of "I should have done something differently" comes up, what is it specifically that you feel you should have done?

client: I think the biggest thing is that I pushed her to keep doing the chemo even when she said she was exhausted and wanted to stop. She lasted a few more months, but looking back I wonder if those months were really good for her, or if I was just too scared to let go and I made her suffer longer because of my own fear. I tell myself I did it because I loved her and wanted more time, but that doesn't stop the feeling that I was being selfish.
therapist: The weight you're carrying in that thought is so heavy — you were a frightened person who loved their mom deeply and couldn't bear to lose her, and now your mind has reframed that love as selfishness, which feels like a very harsh verdict to place on yourself. I want to gently ask: if your mom had been the one watching *you* go through something like that, and she had pushed for more time out of love and fear, would you look at her and call her selfish? What do you think she would say about the choice you made together?

client: I know logically that I wouldn't call her selfish, and part of me thinks she probably wouldn't want me to blame myself either. But it's not that simple — knowing something intellectually and actually feeling it are two completely different things, and right now the feeling is a lot louder than the logic. I guess I'm just not sure that flipping the perspective around like that is really going to quiet the guilt, even if it makes sense on paper.
therapist: You're naming something really important and honest — that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is real, and I don't want to minimize that by suggesting a simple reframe will just switch the guilt off. What you're describing isn't a thinking problem to be solved quickly; it's grief doing what grief does, and the guilt is often one of the ways we stay connected to someone we're not ready to let go of. I'm curious — when you imagine actually releasing some of this guilt, does any part of you feel resistant to that, like letting it go might mean something you're not ready for?

client: That actually stopped me for a second, because I think you might be onto something I hadn't really admitted to myself. If I stop feeling guilty, it's almost like... the connection to her gets thinner somehow, like the guilt is proof that I cared, and without it I'm just someone whose mom died and life goes on. I don't know if I'm ready to just "move on," and I'm scared that's what letting go of the guilt would mean.
therapist: What you just uncovered takes real courage to look at — the guilt has been quietly serving as a lifeline to her, a way of keeping the love visible and present, and that makes so much sense. But I want to offer you a gentle reframe: what if releasing the guilt doesn't mean the connection fades, but rather that the connection gets to transform into something that doesn't cost you so much pain every day — something that honors her without punishing you? What do you think *she* would want that connection between you to feel like, if she could choose?

client: She would have hated seeing me like this — she was always the type to tell me to go live my life, not to sit around worrying. So I think she'd want something warmer, not this constant ache and second-guessing. But I honestly don't even know how you get from here to there — like, what does that actually look like in practice, because right now it just feels like a nice idea that I can't picture myself actually reaching.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you know that about her — that she'd want warmth and living for you, not this — and that knowledge is actually a thread you can hold onto, even when the path forward feels invisible right now. The "how" is something we can work on together gradually, and it often starts with small, concrete moments: learning to let a memory of her bring a smile as well as sadness, or noticing when the guilt voice speaks and gently asking whether it's telling the truth. What's one small way, even something tiny, that you used to feel connected to life or to her that didn't involve pain — something that might still be accessible to you?

client: She used to make this really specific Sunday dinner, nothing fancy, just a roast chicken with these herbs she grew herself, and sometimes I'll catch a similar smell somewhere and for just a second it feels like she's nearby rather than gone. But then the guilt usually rushes in right after and ruins it, so I've actually started avoiding things like that because the crash afterward feels worse than just staying numb. I'm not sure I trust myself to sit with a good memory without it turning into something painful.
therapist: That moment with the smell of roast chicken — that brief second where she feels *near* — that's actually something precious, and it makes complete sense that you've been protecting yourself by avoiding it, because the crash of guilt afterward has taught you that beautiful moments aren't safe. What we might gently work toward together is learning to stay in that first moment a little longer, not rushing past it, so that the warmth gets a chance to exist before the guilt moves in — almost like building a small tolerance for joy without it immediately being taken hostage. I wonder, when that good feeling flickers in for that brief second, what do you think would happen if you just let yourself say something simple, like "there she is" — and let it be enough, just for that moment?

client: I like the idea of "there she is" — it's simple enough that it doesn't feel overwhelming, and something about it feels more honest than trying to force a positive memory. But I'm worried that in the actual moment, the guilt will just be faster than any phrase I try to use, like it's already got a head start. I guess I'm willing to try it, but I don't want to set myself up to feel like I've failed if it doesn't work the first few times.
therapist: It's really encouraging that you're willing to try, and I want you to hear this clearly: the guilt being faster than you in those early moments isn't failure, it's just what a well-worn habit does — it's had a year's head start, and one gentle phrase isn't meant to defeat it immediately, just to exist alongside it. We're not trying to win against the guilt right away; we're just planting a tiny seed of something different, and even noticing "there it is, the guilt rushed in again" is actually you doing the work. So if it doesn't go smoothly the first time, or the tenth time, what would it mean to treat that with the same patience your mom would probably have wanted you to show yourself?

client: That question kind of catches me off guard, because I'm pretty quick to extend patience to other people but I genuinely don't know if I can do that for myself — it almost feels unnatural, like I haven't earned it yet. I think my mom would have had a lot of patience with me, she was like that, but somehow that makes it harder rather than easier because it reminds me of what I've lost. I want to try though, I think — even if I'm not fully convinced I deserve that kind of gentleness toward myself yet.
therapist: The fact that you said "I want to try" — even wrapped in doubt and even while grieving what her patience meant — is genuinely significant, and I don't want it to pass by unnoticed. That idea of not having "earned" gentleness yet is something worth holding up to the light, because it suggests there's a condition you're waiting to meet before you're allowed care, and I'm curious where that belief came from — it didn't arrive from nowhere. What do you think someone would have to do, or be, to deserve that patience in your eyes — and does any part of you meet that bar already?

client: If someone else came to me carrying what I'm carrying — losing a parent, trying their best in an impossible situation — I'd probably tell them they absolutely deserve patience without any conditions. But when I turn that same lens on myself, there's this voice that says I'm a special case, that my situation is different because of the choice I made about the chemo, like that one thing cancels out everything else. I can see logically that it's not a fair standard, but I don't know where that voice came from or how to make it quieter.
therapist: You've just done something really important — you caught the voice applying a double standard in real time, and you named it clearly, which is exactly the kind of awareness that slowly loosens its grip. That voice that says you're a "special case" who forfeited the right to compassion — that's worth examining, because it's essentially arguing that one decision made in fear and love, by someone desperate not to lose their mother, outweighs everything else you are. I'm wondering, if we could put that voice on trial for a moment — what would the evidence actually look like on both sides, the case *for* you being beyond patience, and the case *against*?
